author: Bill Maurer
title: All eyes will be on Apple ( AAPL ) this Thursday afternoon w
text:
All eyes will be on Apple ( AAPL ) this Thursday afternoon when the company releases its fiscal first quarter results for the December ending period. It's expected to be a record quarter for revenues on the back of the high priced iPhone X. Additionally, investors are looking for clarity on how major US tax reform will impact the company's financials, and what management's plans for cash uses are moving forward. Today, I'll preview some of the key items I'm watching in this week's report.
For the iPhone, selling prices may be more important than units: 
Most people will focus on the number of iPhones sold in the period, just as they will with all of the product categories that Apple details units sold for. One reason why unit sales and thus percentage growth or decline over last year's period is less meaningful for me less time around is because last year's holiday fiscal period contained an extra week. Since we don't truly know what that extra week's sales were, we can only average, which creates a bit of a distortion from reality for how unit sales are truly doing. Keep that in mind when considering current estimates calling for 10.7% overall revenue growth to $86.75 billion and EPS forecast to rise from $3.36 to $3.81.
This time around, I'm more interested in seeing how average selling prices do for the iPhone thanks to the high price of the iPhone X. Last year, Apple averaged $694.57 per phone sold, which was up over $7.25 from two year's earlier. That's despite the iPhone SE bringing prices down, but don't forget that we also had the 7 Plus getting a price bump over its prior generation. This year the 8 and 8 Plus were both priced higher than previous models, but Apple also decided to keep an extra generation around of older phones.
Basically everyone on the street expects the average selling price to be well north of $700 in fiscal Q1, but how much higher? Can Apple top the $750 mark, for example, as those $1,000 and higher iPhone X units really pad the average selling price? As I mentioned in an article last week , iPhone X worries have caused analysts to cut their March quarter forecasts a bit, and those numbers continue to come down as seen below.
